==English==
{{wp}}

===Alternative forms===
* {{alt|en|moneth}} {{qualifier|dialectal}}

===Etymology===
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:moneth<alt:mon(e)th>|tree=1}}
From {{inh|en|enm|moneth|mon(e)th}}, from {{inh|en|ang|mōnaþ}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*mānōþ}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*mēnōþs|t=month}}, from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*mḗh₁n̥s|t=moon, month}}, probably derived from {{m|ine-pro|*meh₁-|t=measure}} with moon-cycles being used to measure time. Related to {{m|en|moon}}. Cognate with {{cog|stq|Mound|t=month}}, {{cog|nl|maand|t=month}}, {{cog|nds-de|Maand|t=month}}, {{cog|de|Monat|t=month}}, {{cog|da|måned|t=month}}, {{cog|sv|månad|t=month}}, {{cog|is|mánuður|t=month}}.

Eclipsed non-native {{ncog|ang|calend|t=month}}, borrowed from {{ncog|la|kalendae|calendae}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{enPR|mŭnth}}, {{IPA|en|/mʌnθ/}}

** {{audio|en|En-us-month.ogg|a=GA}}

===Noun===
{{en-noun|+|*<l:UK,_,colloquial>}}

# A [[period]] into which a [[year]] is divided, historically based on the phases of the moon.
#: {{ux|en|July is my favourite '''month'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-08-03|volume=408|issue=8847|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/finance-and-economics/21582498-america-has-changed-way-it-measures-gdp-boundary-problems Boundary problems]|passage=Economics is a messy discipline: too fluid to be a science, too rigorous to be an art. Perhaps it is fitting that economists’ most-used metric, gross domestic product (GDP), is a tangle too. GDP measures the total value of output in an economic territory. Its apparent simplicity explains why it is scrutinised down to tenths of a percentage point every '''month'''.}}
# {{senseid|en|Q5151}} A period of 30 [[day]]s, 31 days, or some alternation thereof.
#: {{alti|en|mo<id:Q5151>|mo.<id:Q5151>|mon<id:Q5151>|mons|mul:m<id:Q5151>|mul:M<id:Q5151><qq:symbols>}}

|passage=Charles had not been employed above six '''months''' at Darracott Place, but he was not such a whopstraw as to make the least noise in the performance of his duties when his lordship was out of humour.}}

|title=[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/15014632.stm Tottenham 3-1 Shamrock Rovers]
|passage=With the north London derby to come at the weekend, Spurs boss Harry Redknapp opted to rest many of his key players, although he brought back Aaron Lennon after a '''month''' out through injury.}}

===Etymology 1===
{{ety|en|:inh|enm:seien<id:say>|id=tell|tree=+}}
From {{inh|en|enm|saien}}, {{m|enm|sain}}, {{m|enm|san}}, {{m|enm|secgan}}, {{m|enm|segen}}, {{m|enm|seien}}, {{m|enm|sein}}, {{m|enm|seiȝen}}, {{m|enm|sugen}}, {{m|enm|sægen}}, {{m|enm|ziggen}}, from {{inh|en|ang|seċġan}}, {{m|ang|secgean}}, {{m|ang|secggan}}, {{m|ang|secggean}}, {{m|ang|seggan}}, {{m|ang|sæċġan|t=to say, speak}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*saggjan}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*sagjaną|t=to say}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*sokʷ-h₁-yé-}}, a suffixed ''o''-grade form of {{m|ine-pro|*sekʷ-|t=to say|id=say}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate with {{cog|frr|sai}}, {{m|frr|seede}}, {{m|frr|sii}}, {{m|frr|sjide}}, {{m|frr|sooi}}, {{m|frr|säie|t=to say}}, {{cog|fy|sizze|t=to say}}, {{cog|gsw|ŝchége}}, {{m|gsw|ŝchegi}}, {{m|gsw|séege}}, {{m|gsw|säge}}, {{m|gsw|sägä|t=to say}}, {{cog|bar|sogn}}, {{m|bar|soon}}, {{m|bar|sågn|t=to say}}, {{cog|nl|zeggen|t=to say}}, {{cog|de|sagen|t=to say}}, {{cog|nds|seggen|t=to say, tell}}, {{cog|lb|soen|t=to say}}, {{cog|wym|ziöen}}, {{m|wym|zuön}}, {{m|wym|zuø̄n|t=to say}}, {{cog|yi|זאָגן|t=to say}}, {{cog|da|sige|t=to say}}, {{cog|ovd|saja|t=to say}}, {{cog|fo|siga|t=to say}}, {{cog|is|segja|t=to say}}, {{cog|gmq-jmk|segi|t=to say}}, {{cog|nb|si|t=to say}}, {{cog|nn|segja}}, {{m|nn|seia}}, {{m|nn|seie|t=to say, tell}}, {{cog|gmq-scy|siğa|t=to say}}, {{cog|sv|säga|t=to say}}; also {{cog|kw|hwedhel|t=narrative, story, tale}}, {{cog|ga|scéal|t=story, tale}}, {{cog|gv|skeeal|t=story; news; narrative}}, {{cog|gd|sgeul|t=story, tale; information, news}}, {{cog|cy|chwedl|t=story, tale}}, {{m|cy|hebu|t=to say}}, {{cog|la|inquam|t=to say}}, {{cog|grc|ἐνέπω}}, {{m|grc|ἐννέπω|t=tell or tell about; speak}}, {{cog|lv|sacīt|t=to say, tell}}, {{cog|lt|sakyti|t=to say, tell}}, {{cog|bg|соча|t=to indicate; to point}}, {{cog|cs|sočit|t=to blame, hate}}, {{cog|zlw-opl|soczyć|t=to accuse, slander}}, {{cog|ru|сочи́ть|t=to emit (a liquid)}}, {{cog|uk|сочи́ти|t=to emit (a liquid), exude, ooze; to drain, sap}}.
{{col-bottom}}

The adverb and interjection are from the verb.
{{root|en|ine-pro|*sekʷ-|id=say}}

====Verb====
{{wikidata lexeme|L381}}
{{head|en|verbs|third-person singular simple present|says|present participle|saying|simple past and past participle|said}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[pronounce]].
#: {{ux|en|Please '''say''' your name slowly and clearly.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[recite]].
#: {{ux|en|Martha, will you '''say''' the Pledge of Allegiance?}}
#* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=VIII|pages=53-54|pageref=53|passage=Then everybody once more knelt, and soon the blessing was pronounced. The choir and the clergy trooped out slowly, […], down the nave to the western door. […] At a seemingly immense distance the surpliced group stopped to '''say''' the last prayer.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[tell]], either verbally or in writing.
#: {{ux|en|He '''said''' he would be here tomorrow.}}
#: {{ux|en|The note I think he '''said''' she wrote is [[nowhere to be found]].}}
#* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=IV|page=46|passage=No matter how early I came down, I would find him on the veranda, smoking cigarettes, or otherwise his man would be there with a message to '''say''' that his master would shortly join me if I would kindly wait.}}
#* {{RQ:Travers Cuckoo in the Nest|chapter=1|passage=She was like a Beardsley ''Salome'', he had '''said'''. And indeed she had the narrow eyes and the high cheekbone of that creature, and as nearly the sinuosity as is compatible with human symmetry. His wooing had been brief but incisive.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1967|author=w:Barbara Sleigh|title=w:Jessamy|year_published=1993|location=Sevenoaks, Kent|publisher=Bloomsbury|isbn=0 340 19547 9|page=95|url=|passage=‘All right,’ '''said''' Jessamy. ‘I '''say''', Miss Brindle '''said''' she’d think about you coming to see the house some time.  I '''said''' I was sure you weren’t the stone throwing kind, not at windows, I mean.’}}
#* {{see more citations|en}}<!-- Please no more than 3–4 quotes here, further quotes only in 'Citations' (see [[WT:QUOTE]])-->
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[indicate]] in a written form.
#: {{ux|en|The sign '''says''' it’s 50 kilometres to Paris.}}
#: {{ux|en|What time does it '''say''' on the clock?}}
# {{rfd-sense|en}} {{lb|en|impersonal|transitive}} To have a common expression; {{non-gloss|used in singular passive voice or plural active voice to indicate a rumor or well-known fact}}.
#: {{ux|en|They '''say''' "[[when in Rome, do as the Romans do]]", which means "behave as those around you do."}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1815|author=[[w:George Gordon Byron, 6th Baron Byron|George Gordon Byron]]|title=The Hebrew Melodies|chapter=They say that Hope is happiness
|passage=They '''say''' that Hope is happiness; But genuine Love must prize the past.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1819|author=Great Britain Court of Chancery|title=Reports of Cases Argued and Determined in the High Court of Chancery|pageurl=https://books.google.com/books?id=YVQDAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA8|page=8
|passage=It is '''said''', a bargain cannot be set aside upon inadequacy only.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1841|author=Christopher Marshall|title=The Knickerbocker (New-York Monthly Magazine)|pageurl=https://books.google.com/books?id=87QRAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA379|page=379
|passage=It’s '''said''' that fifteen wagon loads of ready-made clothes for the Virginia troops came to, and stay in, town to-night.}}
# {{lb|en|informal|imperative|transitive}} Suppose, assume; used to mark an example, supposition or hypothesis.
#: {{ux|en|A holiday somewhere warm – Florida, '''say''' – would be nice.}}
#: {{ux|en|'''Say''' he refuses. What do we do then?}}
#: {{ux|en|'''Say''' your family is starving and you don't have any money, is it okay to steal some food?}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1984|author=w:Martin Amis|title=Money: a suicide note
|passage=I've followed Selina down the strip, when we're shopping, '''say''', and she strolls on ahead, wearing sawn-off jeans and a wash-withered T-shirt{{...}}}}
#* {{see more citations|en}}<!-- Please no more than 3–4 quotes here, further quotes only in 'Citations' (see [[WT:QUOTE]])-->
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[speak]]; to express an opinion; to make answer; to reply.
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare As You Like It|act=III|scene=ii|page=195|passage=You have '''said'''; but whether wisely or no, let the forest judge}}
#* {{RQ:Milton Eikonoklastes|page=63|passage=To this argument we shall soon have '''said'''; for what concerns it us to hear a husband divulge his household privacies?}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|informal|of a possession, especially money}} To [[bet]] as a [[wager]] on an [[outcome]]; {{non-gloss|by extension, used to express belief in an outcome by the speaker}}.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2005|author=w:Ian McEwan|title={{w|Saturday (novel)|Saturday}}|page=192|passage='My fifty pounds '''says''' three months after the invasion there'll be a free press in Iraq, and unmonitored internet access too.'}}

===Etymology 1===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*(s)kend-}}
From {{uder|en|la|candidātus|pos=noun|id=noun||a person who is standing for public office}}, from {{af|la|candidus|-ātus|t1=dazzling white, shining, clear|alt2=-ātus, -āta, -ātum|pos2=participial adjective-forming suffix|id2=adjective|nocat=1}}, in reference to Roman candidates wearing bleached white togas as a symbol of purity at a public forum. {{surf|en|candid|-ate|id2=substantive|pos2=noun-forming suffix}}.

====Noun====
{{en-noun}}

# {{senseid|en|job}} A person who seeks to be [[elect]]ed or [[appoint]]ed to a [[position]] or [[privilege]].
#: {{ux|en|Smith announced he was the party's '''candidate''' for the next election.}}
#: {{ux|en|All '''candidates''' who miss the deadline or make a spelling mistake in their applications are automatically rejected.}}
#* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=Scott Glover, Curt Devine and Audrey Ash|title=Former Florida state senator charged in spoiler candidate scheme|url=https://www.cnn.com/2021/03/18/politics/frank-artiles-arrested-sham-candidate-invs|date=2021-03-18|passage=Artiles, a Republican operative with a reputation for a foul mouth and sharp elbows, is accused of financing a sham '''candidate''' whose candidacy was intended to siphon votes from a legitimate Democratic '''candidate''' in a state Senate race in South Florida’s 37th District. The '''candidate''' has the same last name as then-Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodriguez but did not actively campaign for the seat and has since admitted being recruited as a spoiler.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315084257/https://www.cnn.com/2021/03/18/politics/frank-artiles-arrested-sham-candidate-invs/|archivedate=15 March 2023}}
# {{lb|en|figurative}} A person who is thought [[likely]] or [[worthy]] to gain a [[position]] or [[privilege]]. {{defdate|from 1760s}}

#: {{ux|en|'''Candidates''' must remain silent for the entirety of the exam.}}
# {{senseid|en|suitable}} Someone or something [[likely]] or [[suit]]ed to [[undergo]] or be [[chosen]] for a purpose.
#: {{ux|en|After being presented with various suitors, she decided none of the '''candidates''' were the kind of man she was looking for.}}

|titleurl=http://www.americanscientist.org/issues/pub/2013/3/why-does-nature-form-exoplanets-easily|title=Why Does Nature Form Exoplanets Easily?

|passage=In the past two years, NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope has located nearly 3,000 exoplanet '''candidates''' ranging from sub-Earth-sized minions to gas giants that dwarf our own Jupiter.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807092350/https://www.americanscientist.org/issues/pub/2013/3/why-does-nature-form-exoplanets-easily}}

===Etymology 1===
{{dercat|en|gem-pro}}
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:beggen|tree=1}}
{{inh+|en|enm|beggen}}, of uncertain origin. Possibly from {{der|en|ang||*becgian, *bedcian}}, {{glossary|syncopated}} forms of {{m|ang|bedecian||to beg}}, itself of {{unk|en|title=obscure}} origin. Possibly from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*bedukōn}}, a frequentative verb derived from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*bedu}} (“plea, petition, prayer”, whence {{m+|en|bead}}). Alternatively from {{der|en|gmw-pro|*bedagō|t=petitioner, requester, beggar}}, an agent noun from the same source. Compare {{cog|frr|bēdagi|t=to pray}}, {{cog|got|𐌱𐌹𐌳𐌰𐌲𐍅𐌰|t=beggar}}. All ultimately from the root of {{m+|en|bid}}, which see for more. An alternative theory considers the verb a backformation from {{m|en|beggar}} and derives the latter from {{der|en|fro|begart|t=kind of lay brother}}.

* The singular form {{m|en||ship}} is sometimes used without any [[Appendix:Glossary#article|article]], producing such sentences as "In all, we spent three weeks aboard ship." and "Abandon ship!". * Ships were traditionally regarded as ladies, especially by the sailor, and the pronouns {{m|en|her}} and {{m|en|she}} are still sometimes used instead of {{m|en|it}}, though this usage is in decline.

in negative polarity contexts, such as questions (“Need I say more?” “Need you have paid so much?”), with negative expressions such as {{m|en|not}} (“It need not happen today”; “No one need ever know”), and with similar constructions (“There need only be one”; “it need be signed only by the president”; “I need hardly explain it”). {{m|en||Need}} in this use does not have inflected forms, apart from the contraction {{m|en|needn't|needn’t}}. ** With a gerund-participle, as in “The car needs washing”, or, in some North American dialects, with a past participle, as in “The car needs washed”"[https://ygdp.yale.edu/phenomena/needs-washed Needs washed]" by Zach Maher and Jim Wood, ''Yale Grammatical Diversity Project: English in North America'', 2011 (both meaning roughly “The car needs to be washed”). ** With a direct object and a predicative complement, as in “We need everyone here on time” (meaning roughly “We need everyone to be here on time”) or “I need it gone” (meaning roughly “I need it to be gone”). ** In certain dialects, and colloquially in certain others, with an unmarked reflexive pronoun, as in “I need me a car.” * A sentence such as “I need you to sit down” or “you need to sit down” is more polite than the bare command “sit down”, but less polite than “please sit down”. It is considered somewhat condescending and infantilizing, hence dubbed by some “the kindergarten imperative”, but is quite common in American usage.“[http://www.slate.com/id/2145734 You Need To Read
